item.title: Drill 2026-10-25: reverse a function (rep stosd)
item.description:
# Reverse-a-function drill — 2026-10-25
Target: Windows x86-64 (args in `rcx`, `edx`, `r8d`).
Reverse this short function to equivalent C:
```asm mystery: push rdi mov rdi, rcx mov eax, edx mov ecx, r8d rep stosd pop rdi ret ```
What does it do, and why does it save `rdi` and shuffle `rcx` around?
---
## Answer
```c void mystery(int *p, int v, int n) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) p[i] = v; } ```
An inlined `memset`-style fill of `n` dwords with `v`.
## Explanation
- `rep stosd` hard-wires its operands: store `eax` to `[rdi]`, add 4 to `rdi`, decrement `rcx`, repeat while `rcx != 0`. So the pointer must go to `rdi`, the value to `eax`, the count to `ecx` (the `mov rdi, rcx` must come before `rcx` is overwritten). - On Windows x64 `rdi` is callee-saved (non-volatile), so the function pushes/pops it; `rax`, `rcx`, `rdx` are volatile and free to clobber. - If `n` is 0, the `rep` does nothing; the direction flag is assumed clear (Windows ABI guarantees this on entry).
